summary: An April 1st joke RFC proposing the Internationalized Deliberately Unreadable Network NOtation (I-DUNNO), a notation said to replace readable IP addresses with something harder to read. It pokes fun at people who read, write and misspell IP addresses by hand. It is not a serious protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8771 is an April 1st joke proposing a Unicode notation intended to make IP addresses hard for people to read. It defines rules for turning address bits into UTF-8 sequences and sets levels for how confusing the result should be.

how does rfc 8771 encode an ip address
subtitle: An April 1st joke proposing deliberately unreadable Unicode IP notation.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke says people should not read or write IP addresses directly because addresses are intended for machine use.
tldr.mechanism: I-DUNNO converts address bits into UTF-8 sequences selected to meet one of three defined confusion levels.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8771 is an Experimental joke document proposing a notation for both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

today: RFC 8771 is Experimental and dated April 1, 2020. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The I-DUNNO Proposal
sections.content: RFC 8771 is an April 1st joke proposing the Internationalized Deliberately Unreadable Network NOtation, or I-DUNNO. The document argues that people should use domain names while machines handle IP addresses. It proposes a Unicode-based notation intended to discourage people from reading or changing address text.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st joke proposes making IP addresses harder for people to read. Its premise is that people should use names and let machines handle addresses.

sections.title: Forming the Notation
sections.content: To form I-DUNNO, the IPv4 or IPv6 address bits are written in network byte order and used from left to right to make valid UTF-8 sequences. Sequences may use one to four octets. If the available address bits do not exactly fill the final sequence, the RFC says to add padding bits chosen to maximize confusion.
sections.plainLanguage: The address bits are converted into UTF-8 sequences from left to right. The final sequence may include extra padding bits.

sections.title: Confusion Levels
sections.content: The RFC defines Minimum, Satisfactory, and Delightful Confusion Levels. Minimum requires at least one multi-octet UTF-8 sequence and at least one character disallowed in IDNA2008. Satisfactory adds two of the listed properties, such as a non-printable character or characters from different scripts. Delightful must meet Satisfactory and add two of its own listed properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The notation has three levels of confusion. Each level adds rules about the kinds of characters used.
